title: David J. Taylor and Andy Day

sentences.text: Putney.
Ah, putney.
Putney pies.
Yeah.
How about yourself?
Where are you based?
I am in Somerset.
Usually in London, definitely once or twice during the week, but working from home today in.
Okay, not so sunny Somerset.
So this meeting is being recorded.
Oh, good.
Right.
Well, thank you for getting in touch.
It looks like you've got a great camera there.
Do you do a podcast or you've just got one of the more recent.
It's just a little logitech thing that your computer.
Yeah, it's very good.
Looks like 4K.
Yeah, it's a good one.
Yeah.
I'll have to get myself one.
I did have a logitech actually, but you know, these things are.
They go missing over time when you're moving around.
So.
Yeah.
Let me just get my.
I just sent out a newsletter and somebody called me straight away off the back of it.
So that's good, Good.
Very successful one.
So Brand Gym.
Yes, that's a really good, strong name.
So let me tell you a little bit about us.
I don't know how much you know about us, but we're capital A, so we're an M and A advisory for marketing services companies.
Both buy in the sell side, so we work with investors and strategic buyers helping them find targets to acquire.
Yes.
We also work on the sell side as agencies co, where we have a marketplace for agency owners to buy and sell.
Right.
Just added the option to merge as well, which is the excitement of the newsletter we just sent out.
Yes.
So it would be, it'd be good really to get an understanding of Brand Gym and what it is that you're doing.
I know you've mentioned on your note that you're looking to sell, but obviously it's very nuanced.
So be interesting to know what your plan is and what the timeline is.
Okay.
Okay.
Yeah.
So I think, to be honest, I'd always thought that this business was like unsellable because of the way that we set it up.
But then we were approached by another.
What's that?
We've been approached by somebody else about a potential roll up opportunity which seemed cons, you know, interesting.
But then the more we got into it, we weren't convinced about the people, the people doing it, about their, their real expertise in marketing services.

They seem to be sort of attacking it as a financial operation, you know, so I was, I was trying to talk about the nature of our business and really it just kept coming back to yes, but your EBIT is good and you know, once the deal's gone through, you know, if you want to, you can walk away.
I said well no we can't because we haven't got a team.
So it, the concept seemed interesting but the people, the people we'll be talking to, we didn't feel that they really got what our proposition was.
Right.
Do you mind me asking who that was?
I probably shouldn't, I probably should probably know them already.
It wasn't Ruthbridge, was it?
Yes.
Yeah, brilliant.
I could spot, I can spot anybody's plays.
They're all in the market now.
I come across absolutely everybody eventually.
Okay so I mean you know that, that was, that was, I guess that was.
So we still are having a conversation with them but I mean I think we basically said that the roll up that they're putting together we're going to probably not, not proceed.
So the thing that we've got, and I did drop you a little email before but it was bit short in time before the meeting is that we are, we're an IP led consulting company.
So we started, I started the business 23 years ago and from the beginning it was a virtual business.
No, no fixed costs, no offices and a determination to have no team so no employees.
What we did do, and I started it and then I've now got a partner who joined me about 15 years ago is an IP led approach.
So we've written eight books, we've written a blog which has 1,600 blog posts on it.

We've got an online training academy that I launched during lockdown which we've had over 650 people go through that, that program which is either sold as a custom program to clients or it's an open program that you can join for 995 + VAT per, per person.
So that, that, this year's edition of that kicked off Yesterday actually with 55 people who've signed up to do that program.
So we've got all this, we've got, we've got quite a distinctive brand, we've got a sort of methodology, we've got a philosophy about brand growth.
So it's, it's, it's, it's distinctive but it's, and it's, and it's, it's very boutique and premium.

So I mean David and I who run it, we, you know we have fee income that's, I mean in our biggest year was, was like 1.5 million and then it's probably dropped down a bit now to around roughly 900 to 100, 900,000 to a million with an, if you adjust the EBIT because we obviously just take dividends.
But if you, you know, put in a salary of 100 grand each, we'd be doing say 6, 700 of EBITDA.
So, you know, it's because we have no fixed costs at all, mean just a computer and a paying an accountant.
So it's a.
But, but it's obviously completely reliant on us.
And so we're in a phase now.
I'm 60, David's a couple of years younger.
We're not really in a mode of, you know, being bought as part of an acquisition and then having to sort of, you know, deliver commitment to, you know, increased profitability and growth targets.
And we're just not in that stage of life.
But we have got this asset, you.
Know, and if it's great, genius, that's.
Perfect, it's a great asset.
And if we don't, you know, we've.
And then the other thing, sorry, just to finish, is that we then have a franchise model.
So what we've got is at our peak we had four or five people basically paying to franchise the brand gym and operate as independent consultants, but under the same banner.
We're working together, collaborating, but they are independent with their own limited companies and they pay us a franchise fee.
What's the franchise fees?
You said it's 10 of their fees.
Okay, so they just, they generate the revenue and then.
Exactly, exactly.
We've got a guy in India and a guy in the uk.
Very hard to find the right people because you've got to be a, you know, you've got to be a sort of Jedi level facilitator consultant and be able to win new business and be able to retain clients.
So it's a bit of a needle in the haystack job.
So that's why we have tried over the years to get more people, but it's been, it's been very, it's been difficult.
And so that's why we're down to meet me and David and we have two franchisees who, who are part of the, the team, you know, who pay us a franchise fee.
Right.
And so what's the, what's the core system that you're teaching?
What is the brand?
We, it's brand.
So it's a brand led growth consulting company primarily.
So what we do is we have three, three services.
One is the first one's brand brand positioning and brand purpose works.
That's sort of defining the core, you know, brand idea.
So at the moment, for example, for Heineken in South Africa, on one of Their big beer brands.
We, I've done it for Costa Coffee globally, we've done it for Hellman's Mayonnaise.
We've done it for, you know, big insurance companies.
So that's the, that sort of get that right.
And then we have a thing called Grow the Core which with if you Google after the meeting, Google grow the, Grow the Core as a concept.
This is a whole page of organic results is branding.
Because we've written a book on that and that's a topic that not many people work on.
They'll do innovation, whereas we have this Grow the Core concept.
So that's how do you get more growth out of your existing business?
By making your brand distinctive or by making your packaging better or by activating your brand with a, with an activation, you know, concept and also doing annual brand planning.
So you know, guys, every year, you know, companies do an annual brand plan.
It's typically a pretty sort of Excel based process.
We have like a workshop based process to help people do that.
Sorry, can I just clarify.
So you are offering agency services under.
Yeah, that's, that's 90.
That's 90.
95 of what we do.
90 is probably is actual consulting assignments for clients.
But it's based on the IP that you've created.
Exactly.
So we use those framework, frameworks, models, methodologies, tools to work with these, with these clients.

And then the sort of secondary bit of that is training, you know, training work either through the brand growth program or we've done over the last few years, quite a few where people say we love that program but we want our own.
So we customize it for them and deliver it to the client as a sort of standalone, you know, private program.
So who are the people that it sounds like?
Obviously brands are coming into your, you know, universe, but the, the core of those 55 sign ups are they all individual brands?
It sounds like a lot of them might be agency people that are just learning from you because you guys are the guys.
It's primarily I, I launched it with the, with the idea of making it like a B2C type offer.
You know, the idea of going out and building a program with a sort of, you know, outreach, you know, email system.
And, and in fact what's happened over time is it's, it's actually clients.
So we've got.
So of that 55.
20, 25 is WD40, which is my biggest client I've worked with for 10 years.
So they've, they've put in total about 250 people through the Program including everyone from the board level down and then I've got another 10, 15 from another client and then the odd, the odd.
We've got a Dragon Rouge.
I don't heard of them.
They're a design agency.
They, they've put people on.
Yeah, they put people on every year.
But it's.
No, but it's.
Almost all of it is, is, you know, companies putting marketing people through it.
We've got about maybe 10, between 5 and 10 who, who are like individual sign ups who've basically come through the, either heard of it or come through the email outreach email sequence.
And is it self taught or is there any other.
It's on demand.
It's, it's, it's on demand content.
So eight modules of on demand content which is video that I filmed during lockdown, still going.
And then, and then every, every couple of weeks we do a zoom call.
So people do two modules of on demand content, do some work themselves and then we get the cohort onto a zoom call for an hour and a half where we discuss the previous two weeks work.
You know, how have they got on with their tools, what's, you know, what the questions.
So we do four of those every couple of weeks and then at the end of it they, they graduate and get a certificate.
And this is why it's so dependent on you.
I guess you could train somebody to, to do those calls.
Their expectation is to see you.
Is it?
Yeah, that's the thing.
So I mean it is, it is.

That's, that's why when we had this discussion with this other company, you know, they were saying, well you know, we've got, of the eight companies in the roll up, you know, six the founders are stepping away.
You know, you can do the same if you want.
I kept saying, well no, I can't because there's no one, you know, David and I leave.
There's no one.
There's no one there.
It is me and David.
But what we, but what I, what I was pitching and this is what they weren't very interested in, at least I haven't been up to date.
Is, isn't there a way that I've always thought it, it lends itself as a, as a concept to be scaled, you know, but by someone who wants to scale it.

So if you had a roll up group that had, for example, you know, an insight company, a PR company, a comms agency, a digital agency, a social agency and then the branch in consulting, couldn't it be the brang, you know, group where you've got like a methodology, a philosophy, a point of view, set of tools.
You could train all the agency people with the same methodology.
You could refer, we could refer work to them.
It could become, even become the branch in group, you know, rather than just, you know, united marketing, you know, a no brand brand.

That is the, is the, is the group brand, you know, could it, could it be something that would actually add like an ip, you know, an IP engine if you like, you know, that, that would then help that group be distinctive, you know, and maybe it would be worth, you know, if it would be worth 5% more, I don't know.
And if it was, you know, if it would Normally sell for 50 million, could it sell for 52 and a half million if it was.
If it had this distinctive IP engine in it.
And then is there sort of some sort of value exchange where we could sort of get some, you know, get some value out of our.
What we've created without being in a conventional, you know, setup.
So that's, so that's why I just thought I would.
Because I liked, I like the look because I, I was searching online and you seem to be marketing services specific, which is what attracts me, you know.
So I thought there are a few others.
But we, but we are.
Yeah, very much that.
And so.
Sorry, can I just get your numbers again?
Whereabouts.
Whereabouts are you in terms of annual revenue and ebitda?
David and I combined do about.
I think this last year we did about a million of fees.
So that's actual fee income.
Okay, so that's.
And what's the.
You're saying it's pure profit because you don't have any overhead?
We had what we have.
I reckon we have around 100, around 150.
Com if we combine together something like 150 probably of, of overhead which is, you know, computers, legal fees, you know, bits and pieces.
And then, you know, I.
Then we've then got.
You don't have to take, you know, put it.
We only pay ourselves a minimal salary because dividends.
So put in a, put in a couple of hundred grand, one hundred grand each of salary.
Then you get to sort of 6 sort of 650 of EBITDA.
I worked out.
Oh yeah, of course, yeah.
You know, roughly rough numbers as I say that it, it has been.
We had a bumper year a couple of years ago.
It's very, it's been.
It's very.
Because it's a small.
Because it's dependent on.
We don't have that, you know, we don't have a Huge number of projects.
So you know, we had a couple a year ago where we got, you know, a couple of massive projects and suddenly it was, it was one and a half times that.
But that it's so, so generally speaking.
The, the bulk of your revenue is coming from these consulting.
Yeah.
And then on top of that you are doing the consulting work that's similar to agency work, but you're not, you're not completing it, you're just guiding.
We, we do so our, so our core, what our proposition is the brand strategy piece.
So we.
So for example, in on this project with Heineken, there's an agency partner working on the project and they will take the work on at the end, you know, and then execute it.
But we stop at the strategy level.
We stop when we get to like the brand positioning.
Yeah, well, that's what the value is and that's why you got the huge margin.
So.
Okay, that makes sense.
Yeah.
Okay.
Yeah.
It's complicated because you're not, you're not always, you're not similar to every other agency that might go into a group with you.

So it'd make it difficult to get the leverage from each other unless there was a true integration of the businesses where they did leverage the Brand Gym IP to make it more valuable than it is currently.
Right, right.
So I can, I can understand what the issue is.

I think while you're obviously still doing agency work, I guess consultancy work and the strategy work is still, I mean it's very common in branding companies to do just that, that part and then farm out the next layer to somebody else.
But it does seem like there is something more to what you've got than just an agency approach.
So, so definitely very interesting.
And so where is that conversation got you so far with Rothbridge?
Are you, are you in the roll up and you're ready?
So we've said that, you know, this, this the, the conventional sort of roll up approach where we're just one of the companies that they've got, we don't think is going to, going to work.
But is there, is there a way we are carrying on a conversation to see if there's not some way, some innovative, creative way that we could be part of one of their roll up propositions.
You know, I think it is difficult for them because they're not just doing it in marketing services, they're doing it across a couple of different verticals.
So for them to then pause and treat this one with extra special attention and create a new model for it doesn't Make a huge amount of sense.
Yeah, yeah.

I don't know whether, I mean we had basically said, look, we don't think it's going to work in a conventional way, but I think we're going to have one more conversation to see if there is some way that we could contribute.
So what do you think?
Do you think there's any, you know, more, you know, unconventional way that we could add value to, to something or do you think it's just too, too, too complicated and too difficult to.
I don't think it's necessarily the wrong conversation to be having.

I mean, I've been an advocate for this kind of 360 degree approach to running marketing agencies and I think you've got that and that's kind of to have products, to own the media and the content and also to provide the services and you're, you're kind of doing all of those three things.
So I think as a basis for a business you are in the right direction.

But it's finding a kindred spirit that can understand the value that you've got and also be able to, I guess, you know, sort of guide it without you over a period of time and not waste the opportunity.
I mean, they will need to understand what it is that you have.
But also, I mean they would, I mean, if I bought your stuff, you know, if I bought all of your assets off you and ran it, the problem I would have is that I'm not that guy.
I'm not the agency creative that understands brands.
So while I could do all of the other bits and probably leverage it into other agencies, I wouldn't really understand it.
You.
It's almost like we're looking for almost a one in a million type person.
Because.
What is the name?
So do you, so like the rollup approach?
Is that, is that something that you're currently.
Do you have live?
Yeah.
So we're working on our own roll ups.
The difference is just that this is our, this is our thing.
We've done a ton of them with our partners.
These are the first ones that we're doing without a partner.
But that's because what we're looking to do is give back some of that, that multiple arbitrage that is usually handed to a financial investor or larger agency.

So we're giving that back to the founders so that instead of being acquired for a 5x and then them selling you for an 8 or a 9 or a 10, we're able to roll you up and put you in an acquisition scenario where you're Worth that close to double figure.
So we're doubling the value, then you get that value back rather than an investor taking that three or four times multiple for themselves.
We do take some of that ourselves, but the majority of that is going back into the, the group of founders that come into the roll up.
So we definitely are interested in doing that.
I think the difference is that we would do is we are, we're building them around like verticals or niches.

So we're not, we're not trying to get eight or nine different agencies into bed that are just all agencies because as you know that they can all be completely different in different verticals, you know, working in different industries, et cetera.
So what we would be looking to do is probably work.

I mean it wouldn't necessarily make sense just to find a bunch of branding agencies, but it could be in your instance, because that's what you're doing is to find some other partners that would sort of work alongside you without eating each other's lunch.
Basically, you know, there's already another agency involved in what you're doing that does the, does the delivery.
If we could find a large enough agency.
What we're looking for is, is agencies that are close to 1 million EBITDA.
We're actually $1 million.
So you would qualify for that or you'd be pretty close.
And when you say verticals, like what, what is are there, Are there some that are live at the moment you're in the process of constructing?
Yes.
So we've got an E commerce one for instance.
We've got one that's based on beauty and fashion.
All right, okay.
Yeah, yeah.
So we've got groups of businesses that work well together and that's what we're looking to do.
Whereas other roll ups are just roll ups of agencies and they're just.
Yeah, yeah, cross sell stuff.
Because of the way that we work, we're able to actively, I mean this is all we do.
We speak to like 100 new agencies every month.
We're able to go out and find matches.
And so it's a different approach than most other companies, most other M and A companies because all we're doing is marketing single opportunities and then finding matches.
So we're able to, to create new roll ups in, in new areas.
Once we, we find a couple that are in the same sort of solar system, we're able to like build on those roll ups going forward.
So I was this morning with the guy who is the owner of.
Have you heard of Purple pr?
Do you know Them, they're, they're now in this together group.
They're called a together group.
Yeah.
So I was talking to him about his experience, which is like you say, they're in there in that luxury lifestyle sort of world and that's where they've built their 10 or 13 companies.
So they, like you said, like they share a common sort of solar system as you described it.
Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah, exactly.
So they're doing quite a good job over there.
I mean it is, it's kind of similar to what we're doing as well in that I don't think they fully acquire those companies.
They are putting them into a group to do more stuff with them later.
We're actually looking to do this quite quickly though.
What we're not looking to do is hang on to a business and integrate it for five years and then sell it.

We're looking to find companies, like I say, that already align, do some minimal sort of light pre integration work so that we know what the story is, going into the sales room to get the, the deal done and then we're pitching that as part of it.

You know, that we've already done the pre integration, we know what systems everybody's running on and we've helped the acquirer to align some of those before they actually get into, into the sort of live arena with the, the sellers.
So look, David, this, this extremely interesting.
I've got another call in four minutes.
It's really interesting opportunity but I do think it does warrant some careful thinking.

I would hate to say that you could just be part of a roll up that we're currently doing because I think there's something really special about what you're doing and what you've built and so I'll need to have a think about it.
Oh yeah, have a thing.
I mean there's no, you know, there's no, you know, massive urgency.

I mean we had our annual partner meeting a couple of weeks ago and we all agreed, you know, we were up, we're up five more years of, you know, running the business and we've got enough, you know, enough mojo, enough energy, enough desire to keep going.
So it's not like we're looking to walk away from anything in the next few months or whatever.
You know, we're, we're in it for the next, if the, for the long term.
So there's no burning platform, you're not.
Desperate to get out.
So can I just ask why you wouldn't just go to market on your own?
Obviously there is the value Thing.
But, but because of your ip, would the, would the books and the courses be rolled into Brand Gym if you exited?
Because the IP is worth different multiples than an agency would.
Service businesses are, you know, they're low single digit multiples generally, whereas IP businesses are not.
They can be multiples of revenue and they can be, they can just be made up numbers that people just feel these value that.
I've never, I've never found or never found a way or been aware of a way to, to, to do that, to be honest.
I mean it's only this, this conversation and the one I had with the other company that have, where we started to explore it.
So we've never, we've never practically gone out and tried to do it.
You know, I mean this company found Rothbury's, found us.
We didn't go out trying to look for an opportunity.
So it's only really in the last literally two weeks that we've even thought is there maybe a way that it could, it could work.

So yeah, I think, I think my personal feeling is because you're kind of so different or potentially, I mean I'd have to look into, you know, what it is exactly you're doing and what the percentages are, but it feels like there's another play here rather than just putting you into a roll up with other agencies.
I might be wrong, it might be more straightforward than that.
But it just seems with the IP and the courses, I mean you're saying you've got 55 people signed up, which is, I mean that's amazing.
That's a different type of business.
That isn't an agency business.
I think we would have to find a different buyer.
Somebody that was a bit more savvy around the other bits that you're doing.
Right, exactly.
Yeah.
He appreciates that as a, as a value add.
Yeah.

That's why I always thought it would be like for ex example, you know, it'd be, I always said it's like a, you know, an ad agency, you know, for example, some Chinese, you know, for example, I don't know, ad agency who wants to create a global consulting business.
You know, they want to create like a Kantar consulting type of.
And now basically, rather than starting from scratch, they would basically buy and turn, they would scale the brand gym into a global consulting thing.
Now that's the sort of opportunity I always thought it could be.
Someone who wants to scale it because we don't want to do that.
You know, we're just happy doing our consulting and our work and but you know, it seems we don't do something, the brand will just disappear because we'll just stop one day and then what?
You know, it will just be a bit of a waste really to spend all 25 building.
You need to, you need to have a, a plan together.
It does make sense to be discussing it.

My personal take on it, just like, you know, I've got one minute left is I feel that if you did want to do some kind of transaction, you would be better off going to market, finding a buyer that gets it and it might even be private equity, but it's somebody that can pump money in like you're saying that gets it and can grow it.
And then maybe because you guys aren't ready yet is stay on, roll over some equity into the holding company or the, or whatever and do it for a bit longer.
But we just, yeah.
Pressure on.
On you to, to, to make sure that it works for five years straight without any fuck ups, you know.
So I think that's, that is the play that and I'm just saying that without really knowing everything, but that's okay.
Great stuff.
Great to talk to you.
I'll let you go and do your other call and then let's maybe you know, have a think and then let us know how you think is a good way to proceed.
Yeah, I will do.
I'll follow up with an email in the next couple of days and maybe jump on another call and discuss.
Great stuff.
Thanks Andy.
Brilliant.
Nice to meet you.
Nice meeting you too.
Bye bye.
Enjoy the rest of your day.

summary.overview: The Exploratory Business Discussion meeting between David J. Taylor and Andy Day focused on the potential strategic pathways for Brand Gym, a 23-year-old consulting firm with a significant intellectual property portfolio, including training programs and consulting services. Andy Day introduced Capital A, an M&A advisory firm specializing in marketing services, and discussed the potential for Brand Gym's assets to fit into a roll-up strategy within niche markets. While David expressed a lack of urgency regarding an exit, both parties explored the possibility of leveraging Brand Gym's expertise and methodologies for acquisition by agencies seeking to enhance their value proposition. Actionable next steps include Andy following up with an email regarding potential avenues and scheduling further discussions to evaluate options for Brand Gym's future.
summary.short_summary: David J. Taylor and Andy Day engaged in a discussion about Brand Gym, a 23-year-old consulting firm with an extensive intellectual property portfolio, including training programs and consulting services. Andy Day introduced Capital A, an M&A advisory firm focused on marketing services, suggesting that Brand Gym's assets could fit into a roll-up strategy targeting niche markets. Although David expressed that he wasn't in a hurry to exit the business, both parties explored how Brand Gym's expertise and methodologies could appeal to agencies looking to enhance their offerings. David highlighted that Brand Gym generates approximately £900K-£1M in annual revenue with a strong EBITDA of around £650K. As a next step, Andy will follow up with an email regarding potential avenues and schedule further discussions to evaluate Brand Gym's future options.
